explanations.answer: What will happen to them in days to come
explanations.explanation: Jacob says he wants to tell them “…what will happen to you in the days to come…” (Genesis 49:1). That's the whole agenda, friend. No small talk, no warm-up, just straight to the future. I'd be sitting up VERY straight in that room.

explanations.answer: How his flocks will be divided among them
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't mention flocks anywhere in his opening words. He says he's going to tell them “…what will happen to you in the days to come…” (Genesis 49:1). So nobody needs to bring a calculator to this meeting. This one is about the days ahead.

explanations.answer: Why the whole family must leave Egypt
explanations.explanation: Leaving isn't what Jacob brings up. His words are, “…what will happen to you in the days to come…” (Genesis 49:1). It's a talk about what's ahead for his sons. Pull up a chair, friend, not a suitcase.

Jacob says it right to him: “Reuben, you are my firstborn…” (Genesis 49:3). Firstborn means the oldest son, and Jacob calls him first. He also tells Reuben he is “…my might, and the beginning of my strength…” So Reuben is the one.

Judah does get a big blessing, but he isn't the one Jacob starts with. His turn comes later, at verse 8, when Jacob says, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” The oldest is the one Jacob calls first, and Jacob says, “Reuben, you are my firstborn…” (Genesis 49:3).
Joseph's blessing comes much later in the line, and it's a long one. Jacob starts with someone else, saying, “Reuben, you are my firstborn…” (Genesis 49:3). So Reuben is the oldest son in that room.

The praise doesn't carry through. Jacob says to Reuben, “…you will no longer excel…” (Genesis 49:4). He gives the reason: Reuben went up to his father's bed and defiled it. It's a heavy moment, friend, and I think it stings.

That's what the text says. After the praise, Jacob tells Reuben, “…you will no longer excel…” (Genesis 49:4). The reason he gives is that Reuben went up to his father's bed and defiled it. It's a heavy part of the blessing, and I think it hurts.

Jacob says, “May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly.” (Genesis 49:6). He's talking about Simeon and Levi. Council and assembly, and he wants no part of either one. This is one of the heavy parts of the blessing.

Read it again, friend, because this one is true. Jacob says of Simeon and Levi, “May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly.” (Genesis 49:6). He gives his reason right there: “For they kill men in their anger…” I think this is one of the hard moments in the whole blessing.

Jacob does the opposite of keeping them together. He says, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” (Genesis 49:7). Dispersed and scattered means they'll be spread out. It's a heavy word for these two.

Right, he doesn't keep them together. Jacob says of Simeon and Levi, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” (Genesis 49:7). Disperse and scatter both mean spreading out. It's a heavy part of the blessing.

explanations.answer: Praise him and bow down to him
explanations.explanation: Jacob says, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” and “your father’s sons shall bow down to you.” (Genesis 49:8). Praise AND bowing, friend. That's a double helping from his own brothers.

explanations.answer: Turn on him and drive him out
explanations.explanation: No driving anybody out here. Jacob tells Judah, “…your brothers shall praise you.” (Genesis 49:8). He also says his father's sons “…shall bow down to you.” Praise and bowing, friend, not a push out the door.

explanations.answer: Forget him and leave him behind
explanations.explanation: Nobody forgets Judah in this blessing. Jacob says, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” (Genesis 49:8). He also says his father's sons “…shall bow down…” to him. That's about as far from being left behind as it gets.

Jacob says the reverse. His words are, “Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9). The way he asks it, the answer is nobody. If I were near that lion, I'd tiptoe so quietly even my mustache would hold its breath.

Right, Jacob says nobody is poking this lion. He asks, “like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9). It's a question, and the answer is clearly no one. That's a lion you let sleep, friend.

Jacob says the scepter stays with Judah “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.” (Genesis 49:10). Allegiance means loyalty, friend. So the loyalty of the nations is his. Jacob's words reach way past his own sons.
That's not in the verse. Jacob says, “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.” (Genesis 49:10). Allegiance means loyalty, so the nations side with him, not against him.

Taking the scepter away is the opposite of what Jacob says. His words are, “The scepter will not depart from Judah…” (Genesis 49:10). Nobody takes it away in this verse. It stays with Judah “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.”

Jacob says, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). Wine and the blood of grapes, friend. That picture is all about grapes. My laundry day has never looked like that.

Oil isn't what Jacob says. His words are, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). The whole picture is about grapes and the vine. Laundry day here is a messy one.

Rainwater would be the plain guess, but it isn't what Jacob says. He says, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). The picture is all grapes and the vine. Nobody in this verse is reaching for a rain barrel.

explanations.answer: He bends his shoulder to the burden
explanations.explanation: Jacob says Issachar “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). Jacob first says he saw the resting place was good and the land pleasant. Then he picks up the load. I think that's a man who just gets to work.

explanations.answer: He leaves the land to look for more
explanations.explanation: Looking for more land isn't in this verse. Jacob says Issachar saw his land was pleasant, and then he “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). The text gives him a burden to carry, not a search for more.

explanations.answer: He drives the other flocks away
explanations.explanation: Driving flocks away isn't in this verse. Jacob says Issachar “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). That comes right after Jacob calls him a strong donkey. Bending under a burden is what he does.

That rider is not staying in the saddle. Jacob says the viper “…bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.” (Genesis 49:17). Tumbles backward, friend. A snake in the path, and down goes the rider.
Right, the rider doesn't stay up there. Jacob says the viper “…bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.” (Genesis 49:17). Down he goes, backward. I would hate to be that rider.
Jacob says, “I await Your salvation, O LORD.” (Genesis 49:18). He's speaking to the LORD in the middle of the blessings. It's a short line with a lot packed in.
Pharaoh, Egypt's king, isn't the one Jacob turns to here. His short line is, “I await Your salvation, O LORD.” (Genesis 49:18). He is speaking to the LORD.
Laban, Jacob's mother's brother (Genesis 29:10), isn't in this scene at all. Jacob's short line is, “I await Your salvation, O LORD.” (Genesis 49:18). He's speaking to the LORD.
Jacob says, “Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels.” (Genesis 49:19). The raiders come first, and then Gad turns it around on them. That's a man who doesn't back down.
Gad doesn't run in this blessing. Jacob says, “Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels.” (Genesis 49:19). The raiders show up, and Gad still goes after them.
Nobody's handing over anything here. Jacob says, “Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels.” (Genesis 49:19). Gad fights back. He isn't giving in.
Joseph doesn't drop anything. Jacob says, “Yet he steadied his bow…” (Genesis 49:24). The archers attacked and aimed at him, and he holds steady anyway. That's a tough man.

Right, no dropping the bow here. Jacob says of Joseph, “Yet he steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). The archers attacked him and aimed at him, and he steadied his bow. Steadying it is the opposite of dropping it.

Think of a bow, friend. Jacob says Joseph “…steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). Then Jacob piles on more names: “…the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel…” I'd say Joseph didn't hold steady on his own power, because the Mighty One was holding him.

Abimelech, the king of Gerar (Genesis 20:2), has nothing to do with this verse. Jacob doesn't name any king in his blessing to Joseph. He says Joseph's strong arms “…were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). That's God, friend, so a king was a fancy guess.

Potiphar, the captain of the guard who bought Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 39:1), isn't named here. Jacob doesn't mention any Egyptian official in this blessing. He says Joseph's strong arms “…were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). That's God.
Jacob says the blessings “may…rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the prince of his brothers” (Genesis 49:26). Prince of his brothers, friend. That's a title Jacob gives him right to his face.
Jacob really says it. He ends Joseph's blessing with “…on the brow of the prince of his brothers.” (Genesis 49:26). That's the title he gives Joseph.
Jacob says, “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf…” (Genesis 49:27). Ravenous means hungry for it. Morning he eats, evening he shares. That's a full day's work.

An eagle, friend? That's a good-looking bird, but Jacob never says it. He says “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf…” (Genesis 49:27). Then he says Benjamin devours the prey in the morning and divides the plunder in the evening. WOLF, baker.
A bear isn't the animal Jacob picks. His words are, “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, in the evening he divides the plunder.” (Genesis 49:27). A wolf it is.

That's not what the text says. It tells us Jacob “…blessed each one with a suitable blessing.” (Genesis 49:28). Look back at the blessings: a lion, a harbor, a doe and a wolf. Nobody got a copy and paste.

Right. The text says Jacob “…blessed each one with a suitable blessing.” (Genesis 49:28). Judah is pictured as a young lion, and Zebulun is told he will dwell by the seashore and become a harbor for ships. Different pictures for different sons.

Jacob says, “Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite.” (Genesis 49:29). Fathers is his word, friend. He says Abraham and Sarah are buried in that cave, and Isaac and Rebekah too (Genesis 49:31). So the fathers he means are already resting there.
Jacob says the cave is “…in the field of Machpelah near Mamre, in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 49:30). That's where he wants to be buried. He's looking back to the land of his family.
Close, since the sons he's talking to are brothers, but that's not who Jacob names. He says, “Bury me with my fathers…” (Genesis 49:29). Jacob means the family who came before him.

Egypt makes sense, friend, since Israel settled there (Genesis 47:27). But Jacob points somewhere else. The cave is “…in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 49:30). It's the field Abraham bought, with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah already buried there. I think Jacob is asking to be laid to rest with his family, and that's a tender thing to ask.
Goshen is where Israel settled in Egypt (Genesis 47:27), but Jacob isn't pointing there. He says the cave is “…in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 49:30). That's where he wants to be buried.
Jacob says it himself: “…there I buried Leah.” (Genesis 49:31). He names Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah right before her. It's a family cave, and Leah's in it.
Rachel, Jacob's other wife (Genesis 29:28), isn't the one he names in the cave. He says, “…there I buried Leah.” (Genesis 49:31). Rachel was buried on the way to Ephrath (Genesis 35:19).
Jacob doesn't name Bilhah anywhere in this passage. He says, “…there I buried Leah.” (Genesis 49:31). Leah is the wife he names, right after Isaac and Rebekah.
